text: A metal container of mass 7.9 kg contains 15.3 kg of water. A 1.68-kg piece of the same metal, initially at a temperature of 184°C, is dropped into the water. The container and the water initially have a temperature of 14.4°C and the final temperature of the entire system is 17.8°C. Calculate the specific heat of the metal in units J/(kg K). Specific heat of water is 4186 J/(kg·°C). (862.89099526066 J/(kg K))

scenario.comment:
P16 — calorimetry: the hot piece gives up m_p c (T_p − T_f) to the water and the container (same
metal): m_p c (T_p − T_f) = (m_w c_w + m_c c)(T_f − T₀), so
c = m_w c_w (T_f − T₀) / (m_p (T_p − T_f) − m_c (T_f − T₀)).
The printed final temperature is computed from a hidden specific heat (0.1 °C, as printed), so
every draw is consistent; the answer uses the printed T_f. The constraint keeps the temperature
rise at least 2 °C, so the rounding of T_f moves the answer by at most a few percent.

derived.name: Tf
derived.expr: round((mp * c * Tp + (mw * cw + mc * c) * T0) / (mp * c + mw * cw + mc * c), 1)

parts.answer: mw * cw * (Tf - T0) / (mp * (Tp - Tf) - mc * (Tf - T0))

text: A metal rod A that is 38 cm long expands by 0.065 cm when its temperature is raised from 0°C to 100°C. A rod B of a different metal and of the same length expands by 0.025 cm for the same rise in temperature. A third rod, also 38 cm long, is made up of pieces of each of the above metals placed end to end and expands 0.05 cm between 0°C and 100°C. Find L_A the length of the portion of metal A in the third rod. (0.2375 m)

scenario.comment:
P29 — rods of length L expand by e_A and e_B for the same temperature rise, so per unit length
they expand e_A / L and e_B / L. A rod of the same length with a piece L_A of metal A expands
L_A e_A / L + (L − L_A) e_B / L = e₃, so L_A = L (e₃ − e_B) / (e_A − e_B). Lengths are in cm;
the answer is in m. The printed e₃ is built from a hidden fraction of metal A (0.2–0.8, rounded
to 0.001 cm as printed), so it always lies between e_B and e_A; the answer uses the printed e₃.

text: A 100 kg weight is hanging from the ceiling by a thin copper wire. In its fundamental mode, this wire vibrates at the frequency 429 Hz. You then increase the temperature of the wire by 29° C. |Δf| = f α ΔT / 2 (the source's linear approximation). The weight does not enter the answer.

text: Rods of copper, brass, and steel are welded together to form a Y-shaped figure. The cross-sectional area of each rod is 1.8 cm^2. currents out through the brass and steel rods (same area, which cancels):
k_c (100 − T) / L_c = k_b T / L_b + k_s T / L_s, so T = 100 (k_c / L_c) / (k_c/L_c + k_b/L_b + k_s/L_s)
in °C, and the answer is in K with the source's 273 offset (exactUnit). The end temperatures
(100 °C and 0 °C) are drawn in the figure and stay fixed.

parts.answer: 273 + 100 * (kc / Lc) / (kc / Lc + kb / Lb + ks / Ls)

text: A heat engine takes 0.3 mol of a diatomic ideal gas around the cycle shown in PV-diagram. Process 1 → 2 is at constant volume, process 2 → 3 is adiabatic, and process 3 → 1 is at a constant pressure of 1 atm. The value of γ for this gas is 1.4. scenario.comment:
P150 — cycle 1 → 2 at constant volume, Q₁₂ = n C_V (T₂ − T₁); 2 → 3 adiabatic, Q = 0; 3 → 1 at
constant pressure, Q₃₁ = n C_p (T₁ − T₃); C_V = R / (γ − 1), C_p = γ C_V. The net heat is their

T₃ is that value rounded to a kelvin plus a small offset (−6…+6 K), because the source's
T₃ = 498 K sits 5 K off the adiabat through its T₁ and T₂.
